hook: A phone reviewer tests two brands and finds that 60% of each brand's batteries last a full day. Does knowing the brand help you predict the battery? Not at all, and that is what independence means. A Venn diagram of students in two classes shows the other half of this topic: how to add probabilities that overlap.

prereq.q: Of 40 art students, 15 take Spanish. What is P(Spanish given art)?
prereq.why: Given art, divide by the 40 art students: $\frac{15}{40} = 0.375$.

prereq.q: Events R and T are mutually exclusive. What is $P(R \cap T)$?
prereq.why: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together.

figure.caption: 120 students: 50 take Spanish, 40 take art, 15 take both. The shaded union holds 75 students: 50 + 40 − 15.

chain.cause: Knowing that B happened leaves the probability of A unchanged
chain.effect: A and B are independent: $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$

chain.cause: Put $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$ into the multiplication rule
chain.effect: for independent events, $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$

chain.cause: Add P(A) and P(B) for "A or B"
chain.effect: the outcomes in both are counted twice
the general addition rule: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$

ideas: Events are independent when knowing one happened does not change the probability of the other: $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$. Then, and only then, $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$.
To check independence, compare $P(A \mid B)$ with $P(A)$, or $P(A \cap B)$ with $P(A) \cdot P(B)$, using the numbers.
The union $A \cup B$ is "A or B or both". The general addition rule: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.
A Venn diagram shows events as overlapping circles; fill the overlap first.
Mutually exclusive is not independent: events that cannot happen together affect each other completely.

misconception.wrong: Mutually exclusive events are independent, because one has nothing to do with the other.
misconception.right: If two events cannot happen together, knowing one happened makes the other impossible, so its probability drops to 0. They are as dependent as events can be.

summary: Events are independent when $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$; then the probability of both is the product $P(A) \cdot P(B)$. Check independence with the numbers, never by assumption alone. The probability of A or B is $P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$, subtracting the overlap that would be counted twice; for mutually exclusive events the overlap is 0.
